units.text: Start with the upper setup path. A conformance pack groups Config rules and optional remediation actions for deployment across accounts and Regions.
Now follow the lower evaluation path from the recorder. AWS Config records supported resource configurations in the accounts and Regions you configure.
A resource change or periodic trigger starts a rule evaluation. The result reports compliance or noncompliance; it does not itself block the change.
The optional remediation box uses Systems Manager Automation. Remediation needs a separately configured action and appropriate permissions; a finding alone does not fix anything.
At the far right, the aggregator collects results for a central view. It does not enable recording or remediate resources in source accounts.
Read both paths together: deploy the controls, record and evaluate resources, then assign remediation. Central visibility is useful only when the underlying coverage exists.
Look first at the three accounts on the left. The diagram brings their resource posture into a central Security Hub view.
The center highlights a control finding: an S3 bucket allows public access. Security Hub CSPM assesses posture against the enabled controls.
Follow the finding to the owning account on the right. Investigate the resource configuration and make the appropriate correction there.
The lower workflow begins with enabling a standard, assessing resources, and producing a finding. A finding needs an owner and a triage decision.
Continue through triage to recheck. After remediation, verify the control state instead of treating the existence of a finding as proof of resolution.
The footer separates posture from threat detection. CSPM describes configuration posture; GuardDuty identifies potential threats. Findings flag risk, but they do not block changes.
Begin with the resource groups on the left: EC2 instances, ECR container images, and Lambda functions. Inspector coverage depends on supported, enabled scanning.
The Inspector service performs vulnerability scanning. Check the actual coverage before assuming that an empty findings list means every workload is clean.
The findings panel identifies an affected resource, severity, and fix guidance. Use that evidence to prioritize the work, rather than applying every change blindly.
The central view supports delegated administration across accounts. It brings findings together while the affected workload still needs a responsible remediation owner.
Follow the numbered actions: prioritize, patch or rebuild, then rescan. An EC2 operating system patch and a rebuilt container image are different remediation tasks.
The bottom row makes the boundary explicit. Inspector finds vulnerabilities and can feed findings into Security Hub; Inspector does not automatically apply patches.
At the upper left, the patch baseline defines approved patches. A maintenance window or patch policy determines when and how Patch Manager applies them.
Follow the fleet rollout across development, test, and production. Use staged waves so results from an earlier environment inform the next rollout decision.
The lower diagram follows one managed node. Start with scanning, then install approved patches. The node needs the SSM Agent, permissions, and connectivity.
Continue to reboot only if required, then verify the application and report. Installing a patch is not the same as proving the application is healthy.
Compare the three outcomes on the right. A successful scan reports point-in-time compliance. A reported missing or failed approved patch is noncompliant. No current report is a coverage gap.
Keep the final distinction visible: a failed or unreported node is not automatically healthy. Inspector identifies vulnerabilities; Patch Manager installs approved patches.
Start with the developers on the left. Teams request accounts through a repeatable account-vending process, with the baseline established before workload ownership begins.
The center separates security, infrastructure, and workload organizational units. Account boundaries isolate ownership and help contain the effect of mistakes.
Above the organization, IAM Identity Center assigns teams to specific accounts. A shared access service does not imply that every team gets every account.
On the right, root and organizational-unit guardrails set policy boundaries. Config detects configuration issues; these controls have different preventive and detective roles.
The exception path is scoped and reviewed. A request goes through review to a limited exception with ownership, instead of quietly bypassing the baseline.
Bring the whole design together: centralize the baseline and evidence, delegate safe workload choices, and keep account access and remediation responsibilities explicit.
The upper-left foundation uses Control Tower and Account Factory to create governed accounts. Account provisioning starts the design; it does not finish every control.
The policy ceiling on the upper right separates SCPs for member principals from RCPs for supported resources. These boundaries do not grant permissions by themselves.
The evidence section collects organization activity and configuration visibility. CloudTrail, Config aggregation, and Security Lake support different evidence needs.
In the center, AWS RAM shares supported infrastructure from the owner account. Sharing infrastructure does not remove the surrounding identity and resource access controls.
The lower-right section connects detection to response: GuardDuty, Security Hub, Inspector, and Systems Manager contribute different signals or operational actions.
Finish with the ownership row. The platform team owns the account baseline, security owns controls and visibility, and workload teams own application permissions and fixes.
